abstract.t: This document discusses the drawbacks of the current practice of assigning a UDP port to each multicast application. Such assignments are redundant because the multicast group address already uniquely identifies the data. This document assigns a UDP port specifically for use with multicast applications and lists requirements for using this port. This approach provides immediate compatibility with existing protocol stacks, and this document also defines host enhancements that help safeguard the ongoing cooperative use of this port by multicast applications.

section.title: Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

This document uses the term "multicast group address" to refer collectively to the IP destination address for Any-Source Multicast (ASM) , and the (S,G) pair for Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) , since they serve the same functional purpose. Both exist to identify a stream of packets related to a particular activity. The network's multicast routing infrastructure uses the multicast group address to determine where packets should be forwarded, so that they reach all group members that need them, without being delivered to hosts or networks that do not.

This document describes each separate usage of an application as an "instantiation" of that application. For example, a multicast videoconferencing application may be in use all over the world for a thousand different videoconference meetings at the same time. It would be terribly inefficient (and would defeat the purpose of multicast) if all the meetings were to use the same multicast group, and all copies of the application were to receive all the traffic for all videoconference meetings taking place at that time. Consequently, each instantiation of a multicast application requires its own unique multicast group address. How a unique multicast group address is assigned for each instantiation is addressed by other IETF documents, such as the guidelines for IPv4 multicast address assignment
and for IPv6 multicast address assignment .

section.title: Introduction
section.t: The Internet community has recognized the need to be judicious when assigning port numbers (; ). With unicast applications, the need for explicit port assignment has been reduced by techniques such as locally assigning a dynamic port, combined with some mechanism for advertising that port (; ). Dynamic assignment does not work with multicast applications because it is impossible to guarantee that the port remains unused by all hosts that may want to join a given multicast group. The result is that traditionally each multicast application-layer protocol has requested its own dedicated port assignment. It might seem that even this is insufficient, and perhaps each instantiation of each multicast application-layer protocol should be assigned its own unique port. In fact, this is not necessary.

In the TCP/IP model, the port number in the transport layer multiplexes unicast traffic destined for different applications within a host (; ). With multicast, the use of a port number to multiplex applications is unnecessary because the multicast group address already provides a unique identifier for each application instantiation within a given multicast scope. Techniques like SO_REUSEPORT (details vary depending on the specific network API) already exist to allow multiple copies of the same multicast application to run on the same host and share a single UDP port. This approach is widely used to run multiple independent implementations of Multicast DNS on a single device. This observation is the inspiration behind this specification. If the destination port number is not needed for multicast traffic, and multiple instantiations of the same application can share a single port, then, by the same logic, all multicast applications can share a single port, as long as they cooperate and use the appropriate API mechanisms to share that port. This specification codifies this existing practice, and assigns a single UDP port that may be used by all multicast applications: the Multicast Application Port.
The Multicast Application Port can be used with both IPv6 and IPv4.

Multicast applications can begin using the Multicast Application Port immediately, following the guidance in , on any platform that supports SO_REUSEPORT or an equivalent. In addition, network protocol stacks and APIs can assist in the future development of such applications by enforcing special rules to ensure correct use of the Multicast Application Port. This helps detect and prevent inadvertent application bugs that would interfere with the correct sharing of this port (). Deployment of these special protections is expected to take place incrementally, but applications are free to use the Multicast Application Port without waiting for host APIs to begin enforcing the protections.

In effect, the Multicast Application Port becomes a vestigial placeholder value, present only because the UDP packet format requires a value in the destination port field. At most, it signifies that this traffic is multicast. However, even that information is redundant, since the fact that the traffic is multicast can be inferred by observing that the destination IP address is a multicast address.

Use of this port is optional. There may be circumstances where there are reasons to assign a port via other means, such as when participants cannot meet the requirements in Sections and , or when a firewall blocks a traffic pattern used by the application ().

An application sending multicast messages using the Multicast Application Port as the destination port may also send unicast messages using a different destination port. One possible benefit of doing so is to mitigate the limitations of multicast delivery, particularly on wireless media .

section.title: Multicast Address Assignment
section.t:
The ability to identify a multicast application instantiation by its multicast group address assumes that a unique multicast group address has been assigned to the application instantiation. These assignments are outside the scope of this document. Additional information can be obtained from the overview of the Internet multicast addressing architecture
and the following IANA registry groups:

section.title: Assignment
section.t: This document requests assignment of UDP port 8738 (0x2222) with the service name "multicast-app".

ASM application instantiations using the Multicast Application Port are identified by the destination multicast address. SSM application instantiations using the Multicast Application Port are identified by their (S,G) channel, a combination of source unicast address and destination multicast address . Because unicast traffic carries no such identifier, the Multicast Application Port MUST NOT be used as either a source port or destination port for any non-multicast messages.
The Multicast Application Port MAY be used as a source port by an application that sends only multicast messages.

If any application messages are unicast, then it is RECOMMENDED that the source port used for multicast messages be set to the port to which receivers can send unicast replies. Note that such arrangements would likely require each participant to use multiple sockets, because it must bind to both the Multicast Application Port and its unicast port.

section.title: Application Requirements
section.t: Applications that use the Multicast Application Port MUST meet the requirements in this section.

Application instantiations SHALL NOT prevent other application instantiations from using this port. On hosts using POSIX-like socket APIs , this is typically accomplished by enabling a socket option before binding the socket. Common socket options include SO_REUSEADDR, SO_REUSEPORT, and SO_REUSE_MULTICASTPORT, but the specific mechanism varies by platform.
Applications SHALL NOT send any non-multicast messages using the Multicast Application Port as either a source port or destination port.
Applications SHALL discard all non-multicast datagrams received on the Multicast Application Port.

Furthermore, application instantiations SHALL discard datagrams received on the Multicast Application Port unless they are addressed to a multicast group address being used by that application instantiation (and received on the desired network interface, if specified). Relevant socket API mechanisms such as IP_PKTINFO and IPV6_PKTINFO are described in the Advanced Sockets API for IPv6 and "Socket Interface Extensions for Multicast Source Filters" .

section.title: Host Requirements
section.t: Hosts implementing this specification SHALL require applications using this port to use it non-exclusively. On hosts using POSIX-like socket APIs , this is typically accomplished by enabling a socket option before binding the socket. Common socket options include SO_REUSEADDR, SO_REUSEPORT, and SO_REUSE_MULTICASTPORT, but each platform provides its own method. This requirement ensures that applications developed on a conformant host will follow the correct rules, and therefore also work correctly on older hosts that do not enforce the protections on the Multicast Application Port.

If the application fails to follow the correct steps to share the Multicast Application Port, then the networking API SHALL return an error code, throw an exception, or otherwise fail the application’s attempt to bind to the Multicast Application Port. This helps the application developer discover their mistake and correct it. The networking API MUST NOT try to be "helpful" by silently correcting the misbehaving application and automatically granting it shared access to the Multicast Application Port. Doing so would defeat the goal of ensuring that a properly written application will work both on platforms that implement these protections and on older platforms that do not.
Hosts SHALL prevent use of the port with the wildcard address () by having the socket bind operation return an error code.
Hosts SHALL prevent applications from sending non-multicast packets using the Multicast Application Port as either a source or destination port by having the send operation return an error code.
Hosts SHALL discard all incoming non-multicast packets that use the Multicast Application Port as either a source or destination port.

Hosts SHOULD deliver to an application endpoint (e.g., socket) only packets addressed to the multicast group address(es) that the application endpoint has joined. Technically, this is not essential, since applications are required to discard datagrams received on the Multicast Application Port if they are not addressed to the multicast group address the application endpoint has joined (and received on the desired network interface, if specified). However, for efficiency, it is advisable to perform this filtering, since it is wasteful to deliver packets to an application endpoint only to have that application endpoint promptly discard them.

Some networking APIs provide a mechanism to allow client software to disable generation and checking of checksums for UDP packets
(e.g., the Linux SO_NO_CHECK socket option). Where networking APIs support disabling UDP checksums, this MUST be implemented per endpoint (socket), as Linux does, not as a system-wide default or per-port option. With different multicast protocols sharing the Multicast Application Port, the UDP port cannot be used to identify a traffic flow to determine what UDP checksum policy to apply.

section.title: Firewall Considerations
section.t: Many network firewalls, which operate on network infrastructure, and host firewalls, which operate on individual hosts, are configured to accept incoming messages as long as there was first an outgoing message using the same set of ports . Consider the following sequence of messages:

ol.li:
(Multicast) Host A to group containing Host B
Source Port: 50000 (Dynamic)
Dest Port: 8738 (0x2222)

(Unicast) Host B to Host A
Source Port: 60000 (Dynamic)
Dest Port: 50000

(Unicast) Host A to Host B
Source Port: 50000
Dest Port: 60000

section.t: A host firewall running on Host A (or a network firewall between Host A and Host B) may block Message 2 because Message 1 has port 8738 as its destination port but Message 2 does not have (and is not allowed to have) port 8738 as its source port.

While a firewall could be configured to accept Message 2, this configuration would have to be automated because the use of dynamic ports makes manual configuration too costly even in small deployments. However, this automation leads to unacceptable security risks. For example, if a firewall were to respond to Message 1 by opening up the source port used in the message, a malicious application running on the host could open large holes in the firewall by repeatedly sending variations of Message 1 using different source ports.
Host firewalls could be configured to allow messages associated with a given application instantiation (instead of specific ports), but this approach would not work with a network firewall.

Ultimately, the current practice of assigning each multicast application its own port is more practical for any application that uses both multicast and unicast messages and could be deployed in an environment using firewalls. Firewall configuration with an assigned port is straightforward: allow all messages using that port. However, port-based rules offer limited assurance, because a rogue application can use the same port to masquerade as the legitimate trusted application.

This section records the status of known implementations of the protocol defined by this specification at the time of posting of this Internet-Draft, and is based on the IETF's guidance on improving awareness of running code . The description of implementations in this section is intended to assist the IETF in its decision processes in progressing drafts to RFCs. Furthermore, no effort has been spent to verify the information presented here that was supplied by IETF contributors. This is not intended as, and must not be construed to be, a catalog of available implementations or their features. Readers are advised to note that other implementations may exist.

According to that guidance, "this will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature. It is up to the individual working groups to use this information as they see fit".

Prototypes for Linux, macOS, and Windows are available at . These programs configure a socket to receive messages sent to the Multicast Application Port using a specified multicast address. Another program, such as socat, can be used to send messages and demonstrate, with an unmodified operating system, that the prototype will (1) display messages sent to the Multicast Application Port using the specified multicast address, and (2) not display messages sent to the Multicast Application Port but addressed to a different multicast address.

section.title: Security Considerations
section.t: Firewall and QoS rules that reference ports are typically intended to match specific applications. Because application instantiations using the Multicast Application Port are identified by their destination multicast address (ASM) or (S,G) channel (SSM), rules referencing the Multicast Application Port SHOULD also consider any applicable network-layer address. A firewall rule that only references the Multicast Application Port would match all applications using that port, which is too broadly scoped.

Applications running on a host that does not protect the Multicast Application Port from misuse are vulnerable to a denial-of-service attack if another application claims exclusive access to the port. This vulnerability is not unique to the Multicast Application Port. Regardless of which port an application uses, a malicious application could claim exclusive access to that port first, and thereby prevent the legitimate application from being able to use its port.

Systems that use POSIX-like socket APIs typically have restrictions on binding multiple sockets to the same port. This can serve as a rudimentary security mechanism in that other local applications cannot eavesdrop on the multicast stream. A necessary side effect of using the Multicast Application Port is that applications can no longer rely on this protection. These applications should consider incorporating additional security measures into their protocol. Note that the problem of local eavesdropping is typically no worse than on-path eavesdropping, so it is likely that both attack vectors can be mitigated by the same measure (e.g., encryption).

section.title: IANA Considerations
section.t: IANA is requested to assign the following port:
section.artwork: Service Name multicast-app Transport Protocol UDP Assignee IESG <iesg@ietf.org> Contact IETF Chair <chair@ietf.org> Description Multicast Application Port Reference This document Port Number 8738
section.t: IANA is requested to update its "Application for Service Names and User Port Numbers" to reference this document and ask applicants whether the Multicast Application Port could be used instead. These changes will help applicants understand that a dedicated port may be unnecessary for their multicast protocol.
